# segment


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Rules read prose, but slopometer’s input is markdown: READMEs,
docstrings rendered from notebooks, PR text, chat responses.
Segmentation turns a markdown document into typed blocks (heading, list
item, prose paragraph) that remember where they came from, discards
fenced code entirely, and blanks inline code so that lexical rules never
fire on identifiers. Every downstream stage depends on the position
bookkeeping here: a finding is only useful if it can point back at the
exact file offset it came from.

``` python
from fastcore.test import *
```

A README-shaped fixture exercises everything segmentation must handle:
headings, prose with inline code, a fenced block that must vanish, and a
bullet list. It reappears throughout the later notebooks, and by the
scoring notebook the meter reads it end to end.

```` python
SAMPLE = """# widget

A tool for widgets. Call `enhance()` to start.

```python
enhance(x)  # code is never scored
```

Install it:

    pip install widget

## Features

widget leverages a robust paradigm to deliver results.
It parses the config, then it writes the output.

- fast startup
- fast shutdown
- fast restarts
"""
````

Segmentation delegates block recognition to `mdhtml`, whose `blocks`
function with `nested=True` reports the type, source line span and depth
of every block, including the paragraphs inside list items and other
containers. Segmentation keeps headings and paragraphs. A paragraph that
starts with a list marker becomes an item. Other paragraphs become
prose, including an item’s later paragraphs. Everything else drops: code
blocks and fences, pipe tables, raw HTML, thematic breaks, and block
quotes with everything inside them, since a quotation is not the
author’s prose. A block’s text starts at its first non-space character.
Indented paragraphs inside list items therefore keep the round-trip
property. One class of junk needs handling before the parse. The
`mdhtml` dialect renders out-of-subset tags such as `iframe` as literal
text, on purpose, for paste safety. A scorer sees junk where the dialect
sees text, and a regex therefore blanks every iframe span first,
replacing each character with a space and keeping every newline. Offsets
survive both steps. Each block records the offset its text starts at,
which makes rebasing a finding onto file positions a single addition.

Call `enhance()` to start.'>, <prose @108: 'Install it:'>, <heading @145: '## Features'>, <prose @158: 'widget leverages a robust paradigm to deliver re'>, <item @263: '- fast startup'>, <item @278: '- fast shutdown'>, <item @294: '- fast restarts'>]

The round-trip property is the contract every later stage leans on: a
block’s text is the document’s own text at the block’s offset. The
fixture’s fenced block is gone, and nothing else is.

``` python
for b in blocks: test_eq(SAMPLE[b.start:b.start+len(b.txt)], b.txt)
assert 'enhance(x)' not in ' '.join(blocks.attrgot('txt'))
assert 'pip install' not in ' '.join(blocks.attrgot('txt'))
len(blocks)
```

    8

A list item keeps its wrapped lines and any later paragraphs. A nested
item is an item too. A quote inside an item still drops:

``` python
items = '- fast startup\n  that wraps\n\n  A second paragraph.\n\n  > quoted voice\n\n  - nested item\n- fast shutdown\n'
ib = segment(items)
for b in ib: test_eq(items[b.start:b.start+len(b.txt)], b.txt)
test_eq(ib.attrgot('kind'), ['item', 'prose', 'item', 'item'])
ib
```

Inline code is exempt from every lexical rule: a function named
`enhance` is not a style violation, and `write_docs` itself requires
code symbols in backticks. Deleting the span would shift every offset
after it, and that breaks the round-trip property. Filling the span with
X characters removes the words and keeps the geometry, and the
capitalized dummy token also preserves sentence boundaries: a
space-blanked symbol at a sentence start would make the parser merge two
sentences. All other markup becomes spaces: emphasis markers, link
brackets and targets, HTML tags, footnote labels and math. A URL is an
address, not prose, and link text keeps the sentence readable on its
own. `mdhtml.inlines` decides which characters are text and which are
code, with the parser that renders the document. A finding’s offsets
stay valid in the scrubbed text and in the original alike.

    'A tool for widgets. Call XXXXXXXXXXX to start.'

``` python
test_eq(len(scrubbed), len(blocks[1].txt))
test_eq(scrub('`cmd` runs fast.'), 'XXXXX runs fast.')
test_eq(scrub('Use `` `quad`` for `⎕`.'), 'Use XXXXXXXXXX for XXX.')
test_eq(scrub('See [the docs](a.md) and *this*.').split(), ['See', 'the', 'docs', 'and', 'this', '.'])
assert 'enhance' not in scrubbed
find_decoration(scrub('Works → fine `→ but code arrows are exempt →`'))
```

    [[10] decoration (tell 24, decoration): '→' -> '->']

``` python
tricky = 'Intro prose stays.\n\n<iframe srcdoc="junk px solid">\nmore junk\n</iframe>\n\n| a | b |\n|---|---|\n| 1 | 2 |\n\n> a quoted voice, not the author\n\nReal prose after.\n'
tb = segment(tricky)
assert not any('junk' in b.txt or '|' in b.txt or 'quoted' in b.txt for b in tb)
tb
```

    [<prose @0: 'Intro prose stays.'>, <prose @138: 'Real prose after.'>]

The over-structuring rule (tell 25) uses heading and paragraph-word
counts. Density uses
[`scored_words`](https://AnswerDotAI.github.io/slopometer/segment.html#scored_words)
instead: words from every scored block, including headings and list
items, with their Markdown markers removed. A list item’s findings must
not enter the numerator without its words entering the denominator. Code
and other blocks discarded by segmentation contribute neither findings
nor words.
